title: Cat in a Trap
experiment: Monroe–Wineland Schrödinger cat of a trapped ion (1996)
intro: An atom sits at rest in a harmonic trap, its spin polarized at 45°: half H, half V. At t = 0 a field gradient flashes on by itself for 1.5 time units and kicks H up and V down. Each half now swings in the trap on its own: the atom is in two places at once, and where it is depends on its spin. That is Schrödinger's cat, with the spin as the poison vial and the position as the cat. An analyzer at 45° on the centre of the trap passes only a spin that is still a coherent 45° spin. Key 1 fires the same kick again.
goal: Bring the cat's two halves back together into one atom at rest with its 45° spin, using one more kick (key 1) at the right moment. The observation is at t = 15, through the 45° analyzer.

physics.point: The kick ties the spin to the motion: H swings one way, V the other. A trap brings every swing back through the centre with its momentum reversed, so the same kick, given half a period later, stops both halves together.

idea: In 1935 Schrödinger imagined a cat whose life hangs on one radioactive atom: if quantum mechanics applied to everything, the cat would end up alive and dead at once. In 1996 Monroe, Meekhof, King and Wineland made a small version of it with a single beryllium ion in a trap. Laser kicks that depended on the ion's internal state sent it into two wave packets about 80 nm apart, more than ten times each packet's size, with the position of the ion tied to its internal state.

This level does the same with a field gradient. After the first kick the H half and the V half are coherent states swinging in opposite directions, |α⟩ and |−α⟩. They are far apart for most of the period, and each half carries a record of the spin: the reduced spin state alone is a random mixture, and an analyzer at 45° passes only half of it, wherever it looks.

Is it really a superposition, or just a 50/50 mixture of two atoms? Only interference tells. Undoing the kick returns one atom with the original coherent spin, which a mixture could never do. A trap helps: half a period after the kick each half comes back through the centre with its momentum reversed, so a second kick in the same direction stops both at once, on top of each other. In free space the same job needs three pulses (Humpty Dumpty, level 6-6).
maths: The gradient gives H and V opposite forces ±g for τ = 1.5, momenta ±p with p = gτ = 1.5. In the trap (ω = 0.3, period T = 2π/ω ≈ 20.9) each half is a coherent state: y = ±(p/ω) sin ωt, k = ±p cos ωt. They are up to 2p/ω = 10 apart, against a packet width σ = 1/√(2ω) ≈ 1.3.
